The truth is that man stands before God alone. God as Judge
tears man away from all his natural contexts and sets him in
stark loneliness. Man cannot allow himself to be driven on by
the natural instincts ingrained in his nature, but must choose
his way in responsibility and decision. This is the truth
behind the words: We are indeed His offspring." We are
not nature but Spirit; man has a conscience which calls him
away into solitude.
"In Him we live and move and have our being": for
natural man this word, understood in its true sense, is a
terrifying word, a word which shatters all peace and security
as everyone can know who realizes what it means to live
one's life as in the presence of God. But equally terrible is the
ingenuity with which man, by the illusions of his piety,
conceals from himself the living God who is Lord of heaven
and earth. "O eternity, stupendous word!" we have been
singing. But how ingenious is modern man to misuse the
word "eternal" as a transfiguring description of the achieve-
ments of mankind. On the gate of the churchyard of my
native town there stands an old inscription: "O eternity,
ever abiding!" Well, recently I read something written on
this motto as a theme, and interpreting it as a guiding and
encouraging motif for our cultural achievements. What does
this mean? It means that the eternity of God which limits
and judges our human time-that this eternity is claimed by
man for the religious enhancement of his doings and that
man, forgetful of the judgment implied in the dimension of
eternity, wishes to give to his own actions and achievements
the honour which rightly belongs to God alone.
Modern man to whom the Deity is only too well known
and familiar is further removed from the true God than the
man who in his anxiety and awe of reality did homage to the
unknown God. For God requires this of man, that he should
not exploit the divine for the enhancement of his own human
prestige and glory, but that he should submit to the Lord
and give Him the honour which is His due. Whosoever
